name: Chaoui
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 14 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Idir, Lydia Djamel & Radwan Salim Mahadin. 2024. The Status of Schwa in the Chaoui Dialect: A Non-Linear Analysis. Jordanian Educational Journal (JAES) 9(3), Supplement 1: 1-26. doi:10.46515/jaes.v9i3.868
catalog_locator: pp. 13, 17 and 20-21 of the 26-page publisher PDF (printed folios appear mirrored in the footer as '03', '07', '21', '20'): sec. on the moraic model (p. 13), intervocalic/final geminates (p. 17), affixes and clitics as extrametrical (pp. 20-21).
catalog_quote: [p. 13] Further, the stress phenomenon considers a syllable heavy if its nuclear element is one of the full vowels and light if its nuclear element is schwa. We also claim in this study that full vowels are underlyingly moraic, schwa is moraless, and WBP forces coda consonants to be moraic. [...] [p. 17] Two conclusions can be drawn from this question: word-final and word-medial geminates are inherently moraic, therefore they are heavy and attract stress. In Chaoui, intervocalic geminates are doubly linked to the rhyme of the first syllable where they act as a weight-bearing coda and to the onset of the second syllable where they act as a weightless onset. [...] [pp. 20-21] Under the assumption of WBP, Hayes (1989) suggests that a word’s final consonant is not a member of the prosodic word domain. That is, this consonant is moraless, i.e., it fails to make the last syllable heavy (bi-moraic). For instance, in a noun like [ham.ɣarθ] ‘old woman’, the main stress is on the first syllable.
world_status: statement found in an open source

Locators verified with per-page extracted text: the three quoted fragments sit exactly on pp. 13, 17 and 21 (the printed page numbers appear as mirrored digits '03','07','21' in the footer). p.13: 'Further, the stress phenomenon considers a syllable heavy if its nuclear element is one of the full vowels and light if its nuclear element is schwa.' verbatim. p.17: 'Two conclusions can be drawn from this question: word-final and word-medial geminates are inherently moraic, therefore they are heavy and attract stress.' verbatim. p.21: 'Under the assumption of WBP, Hayes (1989) suggests that a word's final consonant is not a membe…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Only a partial, theory-internal characterisation: syllables with a full vowel /a i u/ (or closed by a geminate) count as heavy and attract stress, schwa syllables are light; a word-final single consonant is extrametrical, so in ham.ɣarθ 'old woman' main stress is initial. No statement of the default edge or of the general locus of word stress is given. A Biskra EFL MA thesis (Elhadi 2022: 24-25, saved) states the same weight principle more explicitly and adds that a word with no heavy syllable is stressed on its initial syllable, but cites no Chaoui source.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the authors' remarks are asides within an argument about schwa epenthesis and moraicity, not a stress description. Derkiani 2023 (another Biskra MA thesis) gives an unusable account equating stress with gemination.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (isolated nouns/verbs from recorded conversational data of 22 speakers from Batna, Khenchela, Oum El Bouaghi, Tebessa and Biskra); no phrase-level discussion; no acoustic evidence for stress.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources fall under tach1249 (Glottolog has no sub-dialect codes for Chaoui). Varieties covered: Aït Frah / Ain Zaatout, SW Aurès (Basset 1961, Penchoen 1973, Boucetta 2026); Ahmar-Khaddou (Mercier 1896); Ouled Soltan/Belezma and Ouled Abdi/Menaa (Torchon in Sierakowski 1871); Ouled Sellem, Belezma massif NW of the Aurès (Joly 1911-12); At Bouslimane of Zellatou/T'kout (Guedjiba 2001); pan-regional urban speakers from Batna, Khenchela, Oum El Bouaghi, Tebessa, Biskra (Idir & Mahadin 2024); Biskra-area students (Elhadi 2022). WALS lists the language as 'Berber (Chaouia)' code bch citing Penchoen 1973a.

sources.note: Syllable/schwa study (22 speakers from Batna, Khenchela, Oum El Bouaghi, Tebessa, Biskra). Stress appears only incidentally inside the moraic argument: full-vowel syllables heavy, schwa syllables light (p.13); geminates moraic 'therefore heavy and attract stress' (p.17); final C extrametrical, e.g. [ham.ɣarθ] 'old woman' has main stress on the first syllable (p.21). No general placement rule is stated.

sources.citation: Elhadi, Wafa. 2022. The impact of the mother language interference (Chaoui) on EFL learners' pronunciation. MA thesis, Mohamed Khider University of Biskra.
sources.note: pp. 24-25 'Chaoui stress': stress independent of word class, depends on syllable weight; goes to the heavy (full-vowel) syllable rather than a schwa syllable; if no heavy syllable, stress falls on the initial syllable. No source cited except Ohsiek 1978 (general); low authority.
